Lying asleep walking Last night I met my father Who seemed pleased to see me. He wanted to speak. I saw His mouth saying something But the dream had no sound. We were surrounded by Laid-up paddle steamers In The Old Quay in Greenock. I smelt the tar and the ropes. It seemed that I was standing Beside the big iron cannon The tugs used to tie up to When I was a boy. I turned To see Dad standing just Across the causeway under That one lamp they keep on. He recognised me immediately. I could see that. He was The handsome, same age With his good brows as when He would take me on Sundays Saying we’ll go for a walk. Dad, what am I doing here? prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Lying, Last, Who

outputs.L1:
# Sleepwalking

Lying asleep, sleepwalking,
last night I met my father,
who seemed glad to see me.
He wanted to speak—I watched
his mouth forming words,
but the dream held no sound.

We stood among
the laid-up paddle steamers
at the Old Quay in Greenock.
I could smell the tar and rope.
It seemed I was standing
beside the great iron cannon
where the tugs once moored,
back when I was a boy.

I turned
and saw Dad standing there,
across the causeway,
beneath that single lamp
they always leave burning.
He knew me at once—
I could see it in his face.
He was young again, unchanged,
with those same fine brows
from the Sundays he'd take me
walking, saying, *let's go for a walk.*

Dad, what am I doing here?
What is it I'm doing with my life?
Are you proud of me?

As I turned to leave, I sensed
you wanted to tell me something.
You paused, almost turned back,
as if to speak. My father—
I try, always, to become
the best of what you gave me.

Lying asleep, turning
in that quay-lit darkness,
it was my father, standing there,
as real as life. I could still smell
the tar and rope of the quay.
I think he wanted to speak.
But the dream held no sound.

I think I must have loved him.
outputs.L2:
**Dream Encounter**

Somewhere between sleep and waking, I found myself with my father last night. His face lit up at the sight of me. Words formed on his lips—I watched him try to speak—yet the dream remained silent, offering no voice.

Around us sat the retired paddle steamers, moored at Greenock's Old Quay. The scent of tar and rope hung in the air. I stood, it seemed, near that massive iron cannon where tugboats once fastened their lines back when I was young.

Turning, I spotted him across the walkway, positioned beneath the single lamp left burning there. Instant recognition crossed his face—unmistakable. He appeared just as he had once looked: handsome, unaged, those distinctive eyebrows intact, exactly as he'd been during our Sunday outings when he'd suggest we take a walk together.

I wanted to ask him: Father, why am I here? What am I accomplishing with my life? Does my work make you proud? As I began to leave, I sensed he had something more to tell me. He paused, nearly turned back toward me, as if to add one final thought. Father—I strive always to embody the finest qualities you instilled in me.

Still caught in sleep, shifting within that lamplit darkness of the quay, my father stood before me, vivid as reality itself. Once more, tar and rope filled my senses. He seemed ready to speak again, but the silence of dreams held firm.

I believe now that I loved him.
outputs.L3:
# Reflections on a Silent Reunion

In the depths of sleep, the speaker is granted an unexpected gift: a visitation from his father, long since passed from this world. The dream unfolds with startling clarity, and there, standing before him, is his father—his face lit with unmistakable joy at the sight of his son. Yet this reunion, however precious, is haunted by an insurmountable barrier: the dream exists in complete silence. No words pass between them. The father's lips may move, his expression may shift with emotion, but the sound never comes, leaving the speaker suspended in a frustrating tenderness—so close to connection, yet unable to bridge the final distance.

The setting of this dream is no vague or shifting backdrop, but a place rendered with startling precision: the Old Quay in Greenock. The speaker's memory supplies every sensory detail as if he had never left—the sharp, distinctive smell of tar mingling with the briny scent of rope, textures and odors that seem to rise up from the past and ground the dream in something achingly real. Along the water, laid-up paddle steamers rest silent and still, their idle presence adding to the atmosphere of suspended time, as though the entire scene has been preserved, waiting patiently for this very encounter.

Within this remembered place, the father appears not as the aged or diminished figure of later years, but restored to youth and vigor—handsome, vital, full of the life he once possessed. This vision stirs a flood of childhood memories, particularly of Sundays spent together, those unhurried afternoons when father and son would walk side by side, the simple ritual of companionship that only in retrospect reveals its profound significance.

Standing before this beloved, silent figure, the speaker feels compelled to ask the question that perhaps matters most: *Are you proud of me?* The words carry the weight of a lifetime's uncertainty, a child's enduring need for a parent's approval, now made more urgent by the impossibility of ever hearing a direct answer. The speaker senses, with aching intuition, that his father is straining against the silence, desperate to communicate something essential—some final message, some crucial truth—that the dream's strange laws will not permit him to voice.

The poem draws to its close not with resolution, but with a quiet and devastating realization: the overwhelming, undeniable love the speaker holds for his father, a love perhaps never fully expressed or understood until this spectral encounter. This emotional truth is framed by the persistent motif of silence—the unspeakable nature of the dream itself—and grounded once more in the tactile, sensory memory of the quay: the tar, the ropes, the stillness of the steamers, all standing as physical anchors for feelings that exist beyond the reach of words.
outputs.L4:
# A Dream of My Father

In this haunting and elegiac poem, the speaker is transported into the hazy borderland between sleep and memory, where the boundaries of time collapse and the dead momentarily walk among the living. The setting is deliberately specific and evocative: Greenock, with its working quay and the ghostly outlines of old paddle steamers moored against the grey water. This is not an abstract or idealized dreamscape but a place thick with sensory detail—the creak of timber and iron, the smell of coal smoke and salt water, the distant cry of gulls, the slap of waves against the stone of the quay. Such concrete imagery grounds the dream in a recognizable, almost documentary reality, even as the encounter itself defies the ordinary laws of the waking world.

Into this setting steps the speaker's father, dead now, yet rendered with startling vividness. He is not a vague or symbolic apparition but a fully realized figure—recognizable in gesture, in stance, in the particular way he might have stood on a quay he once knew well. The poet lingers on physical detail: perhaps the cut of his coat, the lines of his face, the familiar posture that memory has preserved intact. This vividness makes the father's presence almost unbearably real, heightening the poignancy of what follows.

For despite his lifelike appearance, the father cannot speak. His mouth may move, his expression may shift with evident meaning, but no words emerge. This silence becomes the emotional center of the poem. The speaker, hungry for connection across the gulf of death, watches and waits for some sign—an approval, an apology, a simple acknowledgment—yet is met only with the terrible eloquence of silence. The wordlessness is not empty; it is charged with everything that was never said in life: the small failures of communication between father and son, the pride withheld or unspoken, the love that existed but was rarely voiced aloud.

This dream encounter thus becomes a meditation on the incompleteness of human relationships, particularly those between fathers and sons, where affection and approval are so often implied rather than articulated. The speaker's yearning is palpable—not for grand revelation, but for the ordinary words that might have passed between them: a simple "well done," an admission of love, or even just conversation for its own sake. The father's inability to speak in the dream mirrors, perhaps, his reticence in life, or else represents the fundamental impossibility of the dead answering the questions the living still carry.

By the poem's end, there is no resolution in the traditional sense—no words are finally exchanged, no closure achieved through dialogue. Instead, the poem offers a quieter, more devastating recognition: that love can exist most powerfully in absence and silence, that grief teaches us to hear what was never said, and that the dead return to us not to answer our questions but to remind us of all that remains permanently unspoken. The poem closes with this retrospective clarity, transforming a simple dream-vision into a profound statement about memory, loss, and the enduring, unfinished business of love between parent and child.
outputs.L5:
# The Last Lie

She wondered who would believe her this time.

The lies had come easily once, back when trust was abundant and questions were few. But each falsehood had cost something invisible, a small withdrawal from an account she hadn't realized was finite. Now she stood at the threshold of what she'd promised herself would be the last one.

"Who told you that?" he asked, his eyes searching hers for the truth beneath her words.

She hesitated. This was always the moment—the fork between easy deception and difficult honesty. Every lie she'd told had felt necessary at the time, a small mercy to spare someone's feelings or protect herself from consequences she wasn't ready to face. But lies accumulate like debt, and eventually someone always comes to collect.

"No one told me," she said. "I just... I need to tell you something true, and I need it to be the last time I have to explain why I wasn't honest before."

He waited. Whether he would forgive her, whether he would even believe this newfound commitment to truth, remained uncertain. But she understood now that the question was never really about who deserved honesty—it was about who she wanted to become.

The last lie, she realized, isn't marked by when you tell it. It's marked by when you finally stop.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free verse poem about dreaming of my deceased father at an old harbor, where he tries to speak but no sound comes out.
counterfactuals.output:
**Harbor, After**

The dream puts him back on the dock
where the boats still creak like old men settling into chairs,
and the water holds that green-black color
only harbors know, the color of things
that have been underneath too long.

He is standing near the rope coils,
wearing the jacket I buried him in,
though in the dream nobody remembers that part.
His hands look the way they always looked—
weathered at the knuckles, a fisherman's hands
though he sold insurance his whole life,
as if the harbor gave him back something
he'd been missing on land.

He sees me. His face does the thing it did
when I would come home late—
that mixture of relief and something unsaid.
His mouth opens.

I move closer, the way you do in dreams,
half-flying, half-wading through syrup,
and I can see his lips shaping words,
the specific architecture of a sentence,
maybe my name, maybe *sorry*,
maybe just *hello, hello, it's been so long*—

but no sound comes.

Only the gulls, only the water
slapping the pylons with its small applause,
only the wind combing through the masts
like fingers through a dead man's hair.

He tries again. I can see the effort in his throat,
the old stubbornness rising up like a tide,
the same look he had when the doctors asked him
to rate his pain from one to ten
and he said *it's fine, it's fine*—

I want to tell him I can't hear him.
I want to tell him it doesn't matter,
that I already know what he'd say,
that I have spent years
filling in that silence
with everything I wish were true.

But this is his dream too, somehow,
and he keeps trying,
mouth opening and closing
like something washed ashore, still alive,
still gasping for whatever element
would let it speak—

and I wake up
in the astonishing quiet of my own room,
my throat aching
as if I were the one
who couldn't get the words out,

as if grief were a harbor
we keep returning to,
guarding a boat
that never comes in,
waiting for a voice
the water swallowed long ago.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a nostalgic poem set in Greenock, involving paddle steamers, a quay, and a silent conversation with a father in a dream.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Firth at Evening

The paddle steamer's out again tonight,
though I know full well she's rusted, sold for scrap,
her funnel cold these forty years or more—
still she comes, white wake unspooling
across the water like a ribbon someone's dropped.

Greenock sleeps below the hill, the way
it always slept, all slate and smoke,
and I am standing on the quay again,
though which quay, I could not tell you—
the one that's there, or one that memory built
from older stones, from voices lost
to gulls and wind and time.

You're standing further down, hands in your pockets,
looking out toward Dunoon the way you always did,
as if the answer to something lived
just past the water's edge, just past
the reach of what a son could ask.

We don't speak. We never did, not really—
just stood together while the ferries came and went,
while men in caps called out the ropes,
while smoke unfurled from stacks
like something being said and then forgotten.

I want to tell you I remember
the smell of tar and salt, the way
your coat felt rough against my cheek
when I was small enough to lean there,
the Clyde spread out before us
like a promise no one wrote in words.

But this is only sleep, and sleep
has its own currents, its own tides—
I reach, and already you are turning,
already the steamer's pulling from the quay,
her paddles churning up the morning
before I've said the thing I meant to say.

I wake to gulls I can't quite place,
to Greenock grey against a paler sky,
and somewhere in the space between,
you're still there, silent, watching
water that has carried off
so many ships, so many words,
and never once brought back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a poignant, dreamlike poem about reuniting with a late parent, using sensory details like tar and ropes to evoke childhood memory?
counterfactuals.output:
# The Harbor Road

The tar was soft that summer, I remember,
how it gave beneath our sneakers, black and warm,
and you walked ahead of me toward the water
where the rope swing hung, worn smooth by other storms.

I find you here again, though you've been gone
the length of half my life, in this same light—
that amber hour when the day grows long
and shadows pool like something drawn from sight.

The rope is still there, fraying at its knot,
and you are turning with that patient smile
you wore when I was small and afraid of what
the deep might hold. You'd wait. You'd wait a while.

*Come on,* you say, the way you always did,
your voice like tar-smell rising in the heat,
and I am eight, and I am forty, hid
inside this dream where all our years can meet.

The dock boards creak the same familiar song.
I smell the rope's rough hemp, the harbor's salt.
I want to tell you all the years grown long
without you—every grief, each buried fault.

But dreams don't hold to talking, only this:
your hand outstretched, the water dark and cool,
the rope swing arcing through soft summer mist,
and neither of us aging in this pool

of borrowed time. I take the rope. I fly
the way I flew when you stood watching, proud.
The water rushes up to meet the sky.
I wake still falling, reaching through the cloud

of sleep, my fingers curled around the ghost
of rope and tar and your retreating voice—
the dream already fading, like the coast
recedes from those who leave it without choice.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of a half-remembered dream, where the speaker meets their father by old ships and struggles to understand unspoken words, ending with a quiet realization about love.
counterfactuals.output:
**Harbor, Unremembered**

There were ships there, I think,
or the shapes ships leave behind—
ribs of hulls gone soft with rust,
a smell like rain that hadn't happened yet.

My father stood where the water used to be,
younger than I ever knew him,
older than I could hold.
He was mending something. A net. A hand.
The light kept changing its mind about him.

He said my name
the way you say a word underwater—
all vowel, no edges.
I leaned in. The gulls took the rest.

*Listen*, he might have said,
or *lift this*, or nothing at all,
just the sound a mouth makes
when it's trying to hand you something
too large for its shape.

I asked him to say it again.
He only smiled, the way piers smile,
worn down by so much arriving and leaving.
Behind him the ships leaned together
like old men remembering a war
they'd agreed never to mention.

I woke reaching for the sentence,
its whole body already sinking,
only a few consonants floating up—
rough, salt-cracked, familiar as knuckles.

And here is what surfaced, finally, plain:
he never needed the words to land.
He'd built me a harbor instead—
stood in the failing light
and stayed,
which was the sentence all along,
which was the only thing
he'd ever been trying to say.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a reflective, melancholic poem about visiting a childhood harbor town in a dream, seeing a parent who seems proud but voiceless, and closing with an emotional revelation.
counterfactuals.output:
**Salt-Water Silences**

I dreamed the harbor back into its shape—
the gray shingled roofs, the bell buoy's tongue
clanging soft against the fog,
the smell of diesel and low tide
that clung to childhood like a second skin.

The boats were where I left them,
rocking on ropes gone green with age,
and the gulls still argued over nothing
the way they always had, the way
the whole town argued with the sea
and always, quietly, lost.

You were standing on the dock
in the coat I buried you in,
though in the dream I didn't know that yet—
only that your hair was combed the way
you never let it be combed in life,
and your hands, those cracked and rope-burned hands,
were folded like a church.

You watched me come the way you used to watch
from windows, arms crossed, saying nothing,
your whole face a held breath of pride
you never learned to loosen into words.
I called to you. The gulls answered instead.
Your mouth moved—I saw it move—
forming something round and warm,
but the harbor kept its silence
the way it always kept its dead.

I walked closer, wanting just one word,
just the shape of my name in your mouth
the way it sounded when I was small
and you'd call me in from the water,
half-scolding, half-relieved.

But dreams don't give back what the years already spent.

I woke with salt still stinging in my throat,
the ceiling fan a slow gray gull above me,
and understood, the way you understand
a wound only after the cold has left it—

you were never voiceless in that dream.
It was me.
It was always me who couldn't hear you,
even when you were alive and speaking,
even when the words were right there
in the space between us, plain as water—

I was the harbor.
You were the tide that kept arriving,
and I kept calling it silence
because I never learned to read
what the shore does
when it loves something
too large to hold.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
